chapter: Starting out in New York and Chicago
title: Earl Hines as Horace's piano idol
summary: Asked about his piano style, Horace names Earl Hines his idol, recalling Hines' broken bass pattern, 'Sweet Lorraine', and following him in Pittsburgh.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Could I sort of break in here. We've really gotten charged ahead time-wise, I'd like to get back. It's easy to do that. I'd still like to talk a little bit about musical things, even back when you were still at Wilberforce and thereafter. The piano style that you were playing in those days -- was this basically oriented to the stride bass kind of piano?

In those days, my idol was Earl Hines. And I used to watch Fatha whenever I had the chance, you know, because I would see him quite a bit, and he and my brother were very good friends, and they would sit down and talk music, and Earl would play. He loved to play a jam session and things, you know. And this particular 'Sweet Lorraine' (unintelligible) was his bag, deal even in those days. And I don't think of a day now even when I play 'Sweet Lorraine,' (unintelligible) that I don't think of Earl Hines. But he had a bass of broken pattern that he would play, and still keep time. You've got to keep the beat going in your mind,

you know, if you don't, you be (unintelligible), you know? And I just admired the man, you know, and I always loved him, and in fact, as you know, Earl is from Duquesnes, Pennsylvania. And my band was booked in Pittsburgh, even though I was in school, you know. We played Pittsburgh in the summer. And Earl was playing around there, and in those days, there were a lot of jam sessions, and they weren't restricted by the local, you know, like they used to find guys for sitting in, and all those kind of things.

Anywhere that I would hear that Earl, I'd be right on his tail all the time. And I'd watch him. I'd stand right about him and watch these things, you know, it's movin'. And man, he blew so fast some times, you know, I'd want to say to him, hey, can you do that in slow motion, you know? But he was striding, you know. But -- Earl was always my idol, and I'd go back and practice and practice. And I had another guy with me -- excuse me -- that -- during my Wilberforce days in fact, I had two other guys with me left out before -- their names -- one of the greatest guys -- that I think he's a genius -- a musical genius.
